declarations.signature: // Collapse a run of three or more consecutive own-line // comments into one block comment. // Runs at the same indentation with no blank line between them are one comment in intent, so // give them one pair of delimiters. // // Two rules earn their keep here: // // - The delimiters get their own lines and the body sits at the block's own indentation. ktfmt // re-indents a block comment's continuation lines to exactly that column, so this shape is a // fixed point, and whatever indentation the body carries inside itself survives. Aligning the // body past the opening delimiter would not survive: ktfmt pulls it back on the next pass. // // - A run whose text contains either block-comment delimiter is left alone. Kotlin block // comments nest, so an opening delimiter inside the body would need a matching closer and a // closing one would end the block early -- either way the rest of the file is swallowed. // // Run this on ktfmt's output, not its input: the indentation is already canonical, and ktfmt // never gets a second look at what we emit. fun blockifyLineCommentRuns(code: String): String

declarations.signature: @Serializable @OptIn(ExperimentalSerializationApi::class) data class ThreeGeometryPayload( val type: String = "three/geometry", val uid: String, @EncodeDefault(EncodeDefault.Mode.NEVER) val revision: String? = null, @EncodeDefault(EncodeDefault.Mode.NEVER) val sourceBox: String? = null, /** Server-owned document identity for optional camera linking; not geometry identity. */ @EncodeDefault(EncodeDefault.Mode.NEVER) val cameraLinkScope: String? = null, val lines: ThreeGeometryData? = null, val fills: ThreeGeometryData? = null, val points: ThreeGeometryData? = null, val bounds: ThreeBounds? = null, val meta: ThreeMeta? = null, val autoFrame: Boolean = true, /** Per-FLine interactive objects (separate geometry with click/hover callbacks). */ val interactive: List<ThreeInteractiveObject> = emptyList(), val scene: ThreeEditableScene? = null, val editableEnabled: Boolean = false, /** * Measure / section / explode, when the payload came from [Box.threeInspect]. * * `null` for an ordinary [Box.threeLines] payload, and the viewer then behaves exactly as it did * before this existed — no HUD, no clipping planes, no kept copy of the base positions. */ val inspector: ThreeInspector? = null, /** * The scene as [ThreeDrawable]s — geometry plus per-drawable material state. * * Empty for every payload that predates [Box.three], and the viewer then takes exactly the path * it always took: `lines` / `fills` / `points` above are unchanged, and a payload with no * drawables encodes byte for byte as it did before this field existed. * `ThreeScenePayloadCompatibilityTest` is what holds that claim, rather than the comment. */ @EncodeDefault(EncodeDefault.Mode.NEVER) val drawables: List<ThreeDrawable> = emptyList(), /** Explicit same-origin ES modules installed as optional viewer tools; notes cannot load modules. */ @EncodeDefault(EncodeDefault.Mode.NEVER) val toolModules: List<String> = emptyList(), /** * The viewports, when this is a contact sheet. The toy car in `geometry_from_disk.md` is 7cm across, so the grid would be * 140 times its width and the tripod would swallow it whole. The CPU rasterizer draws neither, * and a figure that changes renderer should not sprout furniture. */ @EncodeDefault(EncodeDefault.Mode.NEVER) val helpers: Boolean = true, /** * The frame size this figure wants, in CSS pixels, for the viewer to report to its host. * * # Why the viewer has to say it out loud * * A box output panel sizes itself to its content, and for an iframe it learns the content size * from an `afield-iframe-size` event the iframe dispatches on itself (`outputareas2.js`, * `bindContentLoadEvents`). Every other embedded viewer gets this from `/iframe_autosize.js`; * `threejs_viewer.html` is the one that never included it, because its body is `height: 100%` with * `overflow: hidden` and measuring it would only ever report back whatever size it already had. * * The consequence went unnoticed while the viewer only drew FLines, which want to fill their * column anyway. It became very visible when the mesh figures arrived: a six-panel contact sheet * asking for 855 pixels of height was silently drawn in 430, and each cell came out about a * hundred pixels tall. * * So the size is sent, and the viewer publishes it. `null` means "say nothing", which is exactly * what every payload did before this existed. */ @EncodeDefault(EncodeDefault.Mode.NEVER) val frameWidth: Int? = null, @EncodeDefault(EncodeDefault.Mode.NEVER) val frameHeight: Int? = null, /** * Where the camera starts, when the caller picked an angle rather than accepting [autoFrame]. * * A docs figure chooses its viewpoint deliberately — half of `geometry_from_disk.md`'s value is * that the toy car is seen from the one angle that shows the draped cloth — so the switch from * the rasterizer had to bring [MeshView]'s four numbers with it. */ @EncodeDefault(EncodeDefault.Mode.NEVER) val camera: ThreeCameraSpec? = null, /** Join the document's camera link on load, in this group. See [ThreeSceneBuilder.linkCamera]. */ @EncodeDefault(EncodeDefault.Mode.NEVER) val cameraLink: ThreeCameraLinkSpec? = null, /** Turn slowly about the up axis until somebody interacts. See [ThreeSceneBuilder.turntable]. */ @EncodeDefault(EncodeDefault.Mode.NEVER) val turntable: ThreeTurntableSpec? = null, /** A looping dolly, explode and x-ray move. See [ThreeSceneBuilder.shot]. */ @EncodeDefault(EncodeDefault.Mode.NEVER) val shot: ThreeShotSpec? = null, /** * The view's stored part styles, by [ThreeDrawable.id], for the viewer to apply. * * Set by [ThreeGeometryViewState.update] from the source box's `geometryAppearance`. The viewer * applies them itself, as `applyPartAppearance` does, so that a later style change can be a small * `three/appearance` message instead of this whole payload encoded again. */ @EncodeDefault(EncodeDefault.Mode.NEVER) val partAppearance: Map<String, ThreePartAppearance> = emptyMap(), /** Wire only: where a description's arrays are. See `ThreeWire.kt`. */ @EncodeDefault(EncodeDefault.Mode.NEVER) internal val buffers: ThreeWireBuffers? = null, )

declarations.signature: data class FLineIntersection( /** * Index into the line's `nodes` of the node nearest the click, or `-1` when the client did not * work one out. */ val closestVertexIndex: Int, /** * Where the click landed, in the line's own coordinate space. The three.js output fills in all * three components; the 2D SVG output leaves `z` at 0 — [onElement] is the one to read for a * depth, because it interpolates `z` along the element that was hit. */ val position: Vec3, /** Which kind of element was hit. [FLineHitKind.UNKNOWN] when the output does not distinguish. */ val kind: FLineHitKind = FLineHitKind.UNKNOWN, /** * Index of the clicked line within the lines passed to that one `lines(...)` call, or `-1` when * unknown. The point of it: one shared `onClick` closure can serve a whole figure, instead of one * closure per part. */ val lineIndex: Int = -1, /** The clicked line's [FLine.label], if it had one. */ val label: String? = null, /** * Index into the line's `nodes` of the node that *is* this element: the node itself for a * [FLineHitKind.POINT], the node that draws the segment for an [FLineHitKind.EDGE], the `Close` * for a [FLineHitKind.FACE]. `-1` when unknown. Unlike [closestVertexIndex] this is the element, * not the nearest dot. */ val nodeIndex: Int = -1, /** Which subpath (`moveTo`-delimited piece) of the line the element belongs to, or `-1`. */ val subPathIndex: Int = -1, /** Ordinal of the element among its own kind within the line — edge 0, 1, 2…; face 0, 1… Or `-1`. */ val elementIndex: Int = -1, /** * Where on the element the click landed, `0..1`, or `NaN` when it does not apply. * * For an [FLineHitKind.EDGE], along the segment: 0 at the segment's start node, 1 at its end. On a * cubic this is the **Bézier parameter**, not arc length, and the two are not interchangeable — on * an unevenly-controlled curve `u = 0.5` can be two thirds of the way along by length. It is the * parameter, because that is the number that indexes back into the curve the author * wrote; `FLineHitRecordProbeTest` pins the size of the disagreement on a lopsided * cubic so that nobody has to take this paragraph's word for it. * * For an [FLineHitKind.FACE], the first face coordinate — and [faceCoordinates] says what that * means. */ val u: Double = Double.NaN, /** The second face coordinate for an [FLineHitKind.FACE], `NaN` otherwise. See [faceCoordinates]. */ val v: Double = Double.NaN, /** * Which convention [u] and [v] follow for a face hit — bilinear on a four-corner face, its bounding * box otherwise, or a refusal. Always [FLineFaceCoordinates.NONE] for a non-face hit. */ val faceCoordinates: FLineFaceCoordinates = FLineFaceCoordinates.NONE, /** * The point *on* the element nearest the click, in the line's own coordinate space, or `null`. * * For an [FLineHitKind.EDGE] this is the segment evaluated at [u], which means `z` is interpolated * along the segment: a 3D line drawn into the 2D SVG output recovers a real depth here even though * [position] cannot have one. */ val onElement: Vec3? = null )

One number, not one per axis. */ val scale: Float, /** * The cloud the field was trained to start from, interleaved by [dimension] and already in * the normalised frame — or null if it was trained from a standard Gaussian. * * A particle system has to seed from *this*, not from a Gaussian, whenever it is present. declarations.name: FlowMatchOptions
declarations.signature: data class FlowMatchOptions( /** Gradient steps to take. The dominant cost and the dominant quality lever. */ val steps: Int = 3000, /** Samples per gradient step. */ val batch: Int = 48, /** Hidden layer widths. */ val hidden: IntArray = intArrayOf(64, 64), /** * Hidden activation: `leaky`, `relu`, `tanh`, `sigmoid` or `linear`. * * This is the single biggest quality lever here, well ahead of width or learning rate, and the * obvious choice is the wrong one: on the ring in `FlowMatchingTest`, `tanh` gives samples with * about four times the radial spread of `leaky` or `relu` at equal cost. A velocity field has to * keep growing away from the data — at `t` near 0 the right answer is roughly `-x`, without * bound — and a saturating activation cannot, so it bends the far field back on itself. `leaky` * and `relu` are within noise of each other; `leaky` is the default only because a dead unit in * a network this small is worth avoiding. */ val activation: String = "leaky", /** RMSProp learning rate at the first step. */ val learningRate: Double = 1e-2, /** * Learning rate at the last step, decayed linearly from [learningRate]; null to hold it constant. * * RMSProp rescales the gradient to roughly unit size, so a constant rate keeps taking same-sized * steps however close to the answer it already is, and the fit settles at a floor set by the rate * rather than by the network. This is the cheapest large improvement available here — measured * against a constant rate it took the ring's radial spread from 9.2 to 3.6 and a paired strand's * mean landing error from 3.1% of extent to 0.7%. * * It also decides whether training *converges at all*. At a constant rate, more steps made the * paired case measurably worse — it bounces around the answer rather than settling into it — so * a `null` here turns [steps] from a quality lever into a gamble. */ val finalLearningRate: Double? = 3e-4, /** * Momentum, or 0 to disable. **Leave this at 0 unless [rho] is also 0.** * * Smile applies momentum on top of the RMSProp-normalised gradient *without* the `(1 - β)` factor * that Adam uses, so switching it on multiplies the effective step by about `1/(1 - momentum)` — * ten times, at the usual 0.9. Combined with [rho] and this file's default learning rate it does * not merely train worse, it diverges: the ring test reaches coordinates around 1e23. Momentum at * 0.9 with `rho = 0` is a reasonable plain-SGD configuration; the two together are not. */ val momentum: Double = 0.0, /** RMSProp decay, or 0 to fall back to plain SGD. See [momentum] before changing either. */ val rho: Double = 0.9, /** * How many `sin`/`cos` octaves of the time input the network sees, on top of raw `t`. * * A velocity field's dependence on `t` is often much sharper than its dependence on position — * near `t = 1` the paths have to fan out onto the target's fine structure — and a plain scalar `t` * resolves that badly. Octave `k` contributes `sin(2ᵏπt)` and `cos(2ᵏπt)`, so four octaves is * detail down to about an eighth of the trajectory. Zero means raw `t` alone, which measurably * costs accuracy; past about four the gain is lost in run-to-run noise. */ val timeFeatures: Int = 4, /** * How `x0` is paired with `x1`. * * [FlowCoupling.INDEPENDENT] is the default because it is unbiased and the cheapest. If something * upstream already knows the correspondence, [FlowCoupling.PAIRED] is a different and much * better-posed problem — see its own documentation. */ val coupling: FlowCoupling = FlowCoupling.INDEPENDENT, /** * Standard deviation of noise added to each drawn data point, in input coordinates. * * A finite point cloud is a sum of spikes, and a field fitted hard against spikes will reproduce * exactly those points and nothing between them. A little jitter — a fraction of the spacing * between neighbouring points — turns it into something continuous to aim at. Note that * [flowSamples] can also jitter, and that noise is baked into the cloud once; this one is fresh * every time a point is drawn, which is the more useful of the two during training. */ val jitter: Double = 0.0, /** Seed for the training draws. `null` takes an unpredictable one. */ val seed: Long? = null, /** Override the inferred 2-or-3 dimensionality. */ val dimension: Int? = null, /** Called every [progressEvery] steps with the step index and the running mean loss. */ val onProgress: ((Int, Double) -> Unit)? = null, /** How often [onProgress] fires. */ val progressEvery: Int = 100, )

declarations.name: NeuralParticleSettings
declarations.signature: data class NeuralParticleSettings( /** Names the modules and buffers, so two systems in one renderer do not collide. */ var name: String = "neuralParticles", /** How many particles. A few hundred thousand is comfortable; see the class KDoc for cost. */ var particleCount: Int = 200_000, /** * Frames a particle takes to travel from `t = 0` to `t = 1`. * * This is the integrator's step count and the animation's speed at the same time, which is a * real constraint rather than a convenience: the field is only accurate integrated finely * enough, so a fast morph is a coarse one. Below about 60 the shape at `t = 1` visibly loses * its corners. */ var stepsPerCycle: Int = 150, /** * How long a particle rests on the target once it arrives, as a multiple of the travel time. * * This is the setting that decides whether you can see the thing that was learned. A particle * that resets the instant it reaches `t = 1` is on the target for exactly one frame out of * [stepsPerCycle], so with the phases spread out only a hundred and fiftieth of the cloud is * ever on the shape and the rest — all still in transit — drowns it. Measured the hard way: * at `0f` a 300,000-particle system renders a featureless haze that looks exactly like an * undertrained field. * * At the default of 3 a particle spends three quarters of its life arrived, so three quarters * of the cloud is drawing the learned distribution at any moment and the remainder is the * visible stream feeding it. Set it to `0f` to see the flow alone, or very high to see only * the distribution. */ var dwellCycles: Float = 3f, /** * How far apart in the cycle the particles start, as a fraction of a whole cycle. * * At 1 every phase is equally represented at every moment, so the whole trajectory is visible * at once as a standing stream and nothing ever pulses. At 0 they all travel together, which * reads as a single object morphing. Both are worth having on stage; the default is the * former because it is the one that does not have a dead moment. */ var phaseSpread: Float = 1f, /** Point size in pixels. */ var pointSize: Float = 1.5f, /** Colour a particle leaves the source with. */ var sourceColor: Vec4 = vec(0.15, 0.45, 1.0, 1.0), /** Colour it arrives at the target with. */ var targetColor: Vec4 = vec(1.0, 0.62, 0.22, 1.0), /** Overall brightness. With additive blending this is the exposure control. */ var intensity: Float = 0.5f, /** * How strongly a particle's brightness is weighted toward the end of its journey, 0..1. * * Purely a display weight — it changes no trajectory. It exists because with * [phaseSpread] at 1 the particles are uniform in `t`, so most of them are in transit at any * moment and the destination competes with the haze of everything still on its way there. * At 0 every particle is equally bright and you are looking at the whole flow; at 1 only the * arrivals register and you are looking at the target distribution. The default leans toward * the target, because the target is the thing that was learned. */ var arrivalBias: Float = 0.8f, /** Half-height of the visible region, in the field's normalised units. */ var viewScale: Float = 2.6f, /** Centre of the visible region, in the field's normalised units. */ var viewCenter: Vector2f = Vector2f(0f, 0f), /** * Whether to negate `y` on the way to clip space. On by default. * * Field's 2D world — FLines, and the glyph outlines `layoutText` produces — has `y` growing * *down*, which is AWT's convention. Writing a position straight into `gl_Position` lands it * in a space where the sign works out the other way, so a letterform arrives mirrored top to * bottom. Nothing about the flow is wrong when that happens, which is exactly why it is worth * a named setting rather than a buried minus sign: the picture is a plausible shape, and on a * symmetric target like a ring it is not even wrong. */ var flipY: Boolean = true, /** * Gaussian spread, in the field's normalised units, added to each particle's source point. * * Not cosmetic. A `mixtureSource` field is trained with its source *exactly* on a set of * ellipses — no jitter, because jitter is what broke the curve-to-curve correspondence and * cost a factor of four in landing error. But that leaves only as many distinct start points * as there were training samples, and 300,000 particles seeded from 3,500 of them collapse * onto 3,500 identical trajectories, which reads on screen as a bundle of hard threads rather * than a cloud. * * So: train on the clean correspondence, seed slightly off it. The field is smooth, so a * particle starting a little to one side follows a neighbouring path. Keep this small — it is * extrapolation, and far from the source the field has never been asked anything. */ var sourceJitter: Float = 0.02f, /** Seed for the source draw, so a scene reloads identically. */ var randomSeed: Long = 1L, )

declarations.name: ShaderDlaSettings
declarations.signature: data class ShaderDlaSettings( /** * Prefix for everything this system registers by name: its two modules, their meshes, the * particle buffer, the barrier, and the entries it makes in a render target's pre-target and * module maps. Two systems in one renderer need two names. */ var name: String = "dla", /** * Width of the simulation texture in pixels, which is also the coordinate system the walkers step * in: positions are pixels, not normalised. */ var width: Int = 1024, /** Height of the simulation texture in pixels. Must be positive, as must [width]. */ var height: Int = 1024, /** * How many walkers are in flight at once, one 16-byte record each. Because a stuck walker is * respawned immediately this is a growth rate rather than a bound on the cluster, and it trades * off against [width] and [height]: too few walkers for the area and the cluster takes thousands * of frames to become visible, too many and the whole field sticks in the first few. */ var particleCount: Int = 65_536, /** `gl_PointSize` for the drawn walkers and splats. 1 draws a single pixel each. */ var pointSize: Float = 1f, /** How far a walker moves each frame, along one of the four axis directions. */ var walkStepPx: Float = 1f, /** * How far from a walker the four neighbour probes are taken, rounded and floored to one pixel. * Raising it lets walkers stick before they touch, which thickens the branches. */ var sampleStepPx: Float = 1f, /** * The red value at which a pixel counts as solid. Both the neighbour probe and the age channel * ask this question, so it is one threshold for sticking and for colouring. */ var solidThreshold: Float = 0.5f, /** * The green a walker adds to the pixel it is standing on. Nothing reads green back, and the * preserve pass does not carry it forward, so this is a live view of the diffusing cloud. */ var walkerGreen: Float = 0.12f, /** * The red a walker adds at the moment it sticks. This is the only thing that grows the cluster, * and it is added to what is already there, so a pixel several walkers have found reads above 1 * and takes proportionally longer to decay away. */ var stuckRed: Float = 1f, /** The blue added alongside [stuckRed], so a new branch tip starts with some age rather than none. */ var stuckBlue: Float = 0.35f, /** * Centre of the disc the preserve pass holds solid, in pixels; `null` puts it at the middle of the * texture. Something has to be solid before anything can stick to it, so this is where the cluster * starts. Resolved once in the constructor, unlike the rest of these. */ var seedPositionPx: Vector2f? = null, /** Radius of that disc in pixels. */ var seedRadiusPx: Float = 1.5f, /** * How much red every pixel outside the seed disc loses per frame. At 0 the cluster is permanent; * at the default of 0.001 a branch fades once walkers stop reinforcing it, which is what keeps a * long-running field from filling in. */ var solidDecayPerFrame: Float = 0.001f, /** How much blue a pixel below [solidThreshold] loses per frame. */ var ageDecayPerFrame: Float = 0.004f, /** How much blue a solid pixel gains per frame, up to 1. At the default that is 100 frames to full age. */ var ageGrowPerFrame: Float = 0.01f, /** The blue the seed disc is held at, so the oldest part of the cluster reads as old from frame one. */ var seedBlue: Float = 0.15f, /** * Colour format of the ping-pong target. A float format is doing work here: `solidDecayPerFrame` * at its default is smaller than one step of an 8-bit channel, so an 8-bit target would round each * frame's decay away and nothing would ever fade. */ var format: Int = VK_FORMAT_R16G16B16A16_SFLOAT, /** * Clear value for the target's colour attachment. The preserve pass covers every pixel, so this is * what the first frame starts from rather than a background that stays visible behind the cluster. */ var clearColor: Vec4 = vec(0, 0, 0, 1), /** Seed for the initial scatter of walkers, handed to [ShaderDlaSystem.resetParticles] at construction. */ var randomSeed: Long = 1L )

declarations.name: SmileMdsProjection
declarations.signature: data class SmileMdsProjection( /** * One row per input vector, in the order they were passed, `dimensions` columns wide. The * configuration is centred on the origin and its axes are eigenvectors of the double-centred * matrix, so read distances off it rather than coordinates: the axes have no names and their * signs are not canonicalised. */ val coordinates: Array<DoubleArray>, /** * The retained eigenvalues, largest first, one per column of [coordinates]. A value at or near * zero says that column carries nothing, which is how to find the rank of a configuration: ask * for one more dimension than you think it has and look at the last score. */ val scores: DoubleArray, /** * [scores] normalised over themselves, so this sums to 1 whatever fraction of the structure was * kept. It says how the retained components divide up between each other and nothing about how * much was thrown away. */ val proportion: DoubleArray, /** Which dissimilarity [smileMds] built the projection from, echoed back so a plot can be labelled from the result alone. */ val distance: SmileMdsDistance, /** * Whether an additive constant was applied to the off-diagonal dissimilarities before fitting. * Echoed back, because it changes which matrix was decomposed: two projections are only * comparable when they agree on it. */ val positiveCorrection: Boolean, )

declarations.name: SmileMdsProximityProjection
declarations.signature: data class SmileMdsProximityProjection( /** * One row per row of the distance matrix, in its order, `dimensions` columns wide. A value at or near * zero says that column carries nothing, which is how to find the rank of whatever the matrix * describes. */ val scores: DoubleArray, /** * [scores] normalised over themselves, so this sums to 1 whatever fraction of the structure was * kept. For how much a two-dimensional picture actually lost, compare its distances against the * matrix you supplied; `public/docs/projection_examples.md` does that with a stress figure. */ val proportion: DoubleArray, /** * Whatever you passed to [smileMdsDistances], carried through untouched. Nothing in the fit reads * it: it is here so a box holding several projections can tell which matrix each came from. */ val label: String, /** * Whether an additive constant was applied to the off-diagonal dissimilarities before fitting. * A distance that is a metric is not thereby Euclidean, and an edit distance or a hop count * usually needs this on before classical MDS has more than a couple of usable dimensions. */ val positiveCorrection: Boolean, )

declarations.signature: data class SmileTsneProjection( /** * One row per input vector, in the order they were passed, `dimensions` columns wide, and * zero-mean by column because Smile subtracts the column means as its last step. What survives * here is which points are near which; the axes and the distance between two separated groups do * not, and `public/docs/projection_examples.md` measures the gap between the true ratio of two * cluster separations and the one a t-SNE plot of them shows. */ val coordinates: Array<DoubleArray>, /** * Smile's Kullback-Leibler divergence between the input affinities and the projected ones, in * bits, as last measured rather than as minimised: the fit evaluates it every tenth iteration and * returns the final evaluation, not the best one it saw. It compares iterations within one fit * and does not rank two fits against each other. * * Two seeds can reach costs that agree to several decimals and pictures that share nothing, which * `public/docs/projection_examples.md` measures both halves of. */ val cost: Double, /** * Which dissimilarity the vectors were reduced to before fitting. `EUCLIDEAN` hands Smile the * vectors and lets it compute distances itself; `COSINE` hands it a cosine-distance matrix Field * built first. */ val distance: SmileMdsDistance, /** * The perplexity this fit ran at. A t-SNE plot cannot be read without it, since it is the dial * between keeping local neighbourhoods and keeping the distance between clusters, and it is * carried here so a caption can be written from the result. */ val perplexity: Double, /** * The seed installed in Smile's process-wide random source for this fit. Two fits of the same * input at the same seed are bit-identical; two at different seeds are two equally good answers * that look nothing alike, so the seed belongs in the caption of a figure anyone else will read. */ val seed: Long, )

declarations.name: SweepConfig
declarations.signature: @Serializable data class SweepConfig( /** Root of the run's randomness. Every render draws from `seed` and its own index, nothing else. */ val seed: Long = 1L, /** How many renders to attempt. Left unbounded, [maxDurationMs] or the disk floor ends the run. */ val count: Int = Int.MAX_VALUE, /** Which files under the pool directory are keys. See [everyKeyGlob], and `keyFilesMatching`. */ val pattern: String = everyKeyGlob, /** * Fewest keys in one blend. `1` is meaningful and worth allowing: a blend of one key is that key * replayed exactly, which salts the archive with unmixed references to compare the blends against. */ val minArity: Int = 2, /** Most keys in one blend, clamped to the pool size. */ val maxArity: Int = 3, /** * The Dirichlet concentration the weights are drawn from, and the single most consequential * number here. * * At `1.0` the weights are uniform over the simplex. Below it they bunch into the corners, so a * blend is mostly one key with the others as perturbation — the setting for a night that should * stay recognisable. Well above it they even out, and every blend is the average of its * participants, which for a dense pool means a night of mush. Start at `0.6` if the point is * variety you can still attribute. */ val concentration: Double = 1.0, /** * How often a blend is pushed outside the hull of its participants. * * An extrapolated look is the one a person would not have authored: past the end of every key * you saved rather than between them. It is also where a look most often falls apart, which is * why this is a fraction of the night rather than all of it. */ val extrapolationProbability: Double = 0.15, /** * Least push, measured in hull-crossings from the anchor. * * `1.0` lands exactly on the far face of the hull — the anchor's own weight passes through zero * there — so `1.2` is a fifth of the way again beyond it. Below `1.0` would be inside the hull * and is refused, because a "gain" that sometimes extrapolated and sometimes did not would make * the archive's `extrapolationGain` field mean nothing. */ val minExtrapolationGain: Double = 1.2, /** Most push. Past about `3.0` most looks fall apart, which is occasionally the point. */ val maxExtrapolationGain: Double = 2.0, /** See [DiscreteBlend]. */ val discrete: DiscreteBlend = DiscreteBlend.ANCHOR, /** See [MissingSlots]. */ val missingSlots: MissingSlots = MissingSlots.FILL_FROM_LIVE, /** * Round each blended number back to the numeric type the anchor held it in. * * On by default because [KeyframeScope.interpolate] returns `Double` unless *both* sides were * `Float`, so an `Int` lane — an instance count, a subdivision level — comes back as a `Double` * that an `Int` uniform will refuse. Turn it off only to see the unrounded trajectory. * * Rounded, **not** clamped. An extrapolated blend can put an `Int` lane outside the range its * `intTarget` declares — 14 instances where 9 is the maximum — and the clamp stays where it * already lives, in the target, on apply. So the key records the point in the space that was * actually visited *and* still reproduces the render exactly; clamping in the key would lose the * first without gaining the second. */ val preserveNumericKind: Boolean = true, /** Write the blend to the live scope before calling the callback. Off makes the sweep a pure generator. */ val applyToScope: Boolean = true, /** * Put the scope back the way it was found when the run ends, however it ends. * * The restore is a `capture()` taken before the first render and invoked in a `finally`, so it * inherits `capture`'s own caveat: a key holds the *values* it read, not copies, and a target * registered with a bare getter can therefore hand it the live mutable vector rather than a * snapshot of one. The typed registrations ([KeyframeScope.vector3Target] and friends) copy in * both directions and are safe; a hand-rolled `target(name, get, set)` over a `Vector3f` is the * shape to check before trusting this. */ val restoreScopeAtEnd: Boolean = true, /** Wall-clock budget in milliseconds; `0` for none. The "stop at 7am" knob. */ val maxDurationMs: Long = 0, /** * Stop while this many bytes are still free on the archive's filesystem. Eight gigabytes by * default, which is generous on purpose: an overnight sweep of GPU stills is a *rate* of disk * consumption, and the thing that goes wrong is not the archive being large but the machine * having nothing left at 4am. */ val minFreeBytes: Long = 8L shl 30, /** Consecutive failures that mean the night is broken rather than the render unlucky. */ val maxConsecutiveFailures: Int = 5, /** Skip renders a previous process already finished. See [KeyframeSweep.run]. */ val resume: Boolean = true, /** Keep the directory of a failed render, with its manifest and partial output, for forensics. */ val keepFailedRenders: Boolean = true )

declarations.name: VecNNBuildOptions
declarations.signature: data class VecNNBuildOptions( /** * Width of the LSH random projections, in the same units as your point coordinates. Wider * buckets collect more points, so a query considers more candidates and is likelier to find the * true neighbours, at more work per query; narrower buckets are cheaper and miss more. Must be * finite and greater than zero. * * The default of 1.0 suits points near unit scale and is far too narrow for, say, screen * coordinates — there almost every query ends up in the brute-force fallback instead. */ val lshBucketWidth: Double = 1.0, /** * How many random projections make up one LSH hash value. More projections mean more selective * buckets, which is the same trade as a narrower [lshBucketWidth]: fewer candidates examined, * more true neighbours missed. Must be greater than zero. */ val lshProjectionCount: Int = 8, /** * Size of the universal hash table behind each LSH hash; the default 9973 is prime. Bigger costs * memory and reduces accidental collisions between unrelated buckets. Must be greater than zero. */ val lshUniversalHashSize: Int = 9973, /** * Leave this true and duplicate points are indexed normally, simply showing up as several * neighbours at the same distance. Set it false and [vec2NN] / [vec3NN] reject any list holding * two bit-for-bit identical points, with an `IllegalArgumentException` naming the offending * index. Note that this compares raw coordinate bits, so `0.0` and `-0.0` count as different * points. */ val allowDuplicatePoints: Boolean = true )
